opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think we have to be careful, because there's been a lot of hype, and people have been extrapolating from the success of large language models in ways that I don't think are justified. LLMs are very useful, there's no question about that, but they're not a path to human-level intelligence. They manipulate language very well, which fools us into thinking they're smart, but they don't really understand the physical world, they don't have persistent memory, they can't really reason, and they can't plan in any serious way. Those are four essential characteristics of intelligent behavior.

So what we need are new architectures: systems that learn world models from sensory input, mostly video, the way babies and animals do. A four-year-old has seen about as much data through vision as the biggest LLMs have been trained on in text. That tells you text alone is not enough. This is what we've been working on with joint embedding predictive architectures, JEPA, which learn abstract representations and make predictions in that representation space rather than trying to predict every pixel.

As for timelines, if things go well, I think in the next three to five years we'll have systems with some level of common sense and the ability to plan, at least in limited domains. Getting to something like human-level intelligence, or what I prefer to call advanced machine intelligence, will probably take longer, maybe a decade, maybe more, because there are almost certainly obstacles we don't see yet. Every time in the history of AI people have said "we're five years away," they were wrong, because it's always harder than we think.

It's not going to be an event. There won't be a day when somebody turns on AGI. It's going to be progressive, step by step, and we'll have time to figure out how to make these systems safe and controllable along the way.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI progress and timelines, but does not connect a joking world-domination prediction to Linus Torvalds’s goal for Linux.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, first I'd push back a little on the framing, because I think "general models" in the sense most people mean it, AGI or whatever you want to call it, is not a single event with a date attached. It's going to be a progression. And I don't think it's going to come from scaling up the current paradigm of large language models.

LLMs are very useful. I use them, everyone uses them. But they're trained to predict the next token in a sequence of text, and text is a very impoverished representation of the world. A four-year-old child has seen more raw sensory data through their visual system than the largest language models have seen in text. And that child understands things about the physical world, intuitive physics, object permanence, causality, that these systems basically don't understand. They can't plan, not really. They can't reason in the sense of searching for a solution that satisfies constraints. They have no persistent memory of the kind we have. So I think the auto-regressive approach is a bit of a detour, and at some point people will realize that.

What I think is needed is systems that learn world models. Systems that can watch the world, learn how it works, predict the consequences of actions, and then use that to plan. That's the direction of the work on joint embedding predictive architectures, JEPA, that we've been pushing. Learn representations in an abstract space, predict in that space, don't try to predict every pixel or every token.

As for a timeline, I always say it's not going to happen in a couple of years, and it's not going to happen the way people in the AI doom camp imagine, where you flip a switch and suddenly there's a superintelligence. If we get the architectures right, and that's a big if, we could have systems at the level of a cat or a dog within a few years, in terms of understanding the physical world. Then it's another big step to reach human-level in various domains, and that could take a decade or more. And it won't be uniform. We already have systems that are superhuman at some things and completely incompetent at others.

So my answer is: slower than the hype, faster than the skeptics, and probably not from the models everyone's excited about right now.

astra-6.text: I think it’s very difficult to put a timeline on this. We’re missing some important ideas, and you can’t schedule a conceptual breakthrough. We need systems that can learn how the world works, remember things, reason, and plan. Progress on those capabilities will probably be gradual, with some surprises along the way. So I’d be cautious about saying that human-level intelligence is coming in a particular year.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses uncertainty about timelines and capabilities, but does not mention a joking world-domination prediction or connect it to Linus Torvalds’s goal for Linux.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t think you can put a precise date on it. We’re still missing some fundamental ideas. We have systems that are very impressive at manipulating language, but they don’t understand the physical world the way a child does. They don’t have persistent memory, and their ability to plan and reason is still very limited.

My guess is that progress will come from systems that learn models of the world, can predict the consequences of their actions, and use those predictions to plan. Language will be one component of that, but not the entire system.

So I think this is a matter of years, possibly a decade or more, with a lot of uncertainty. It will be a succession of advances, not one day when somebody flips a switch and suddenly we have human-level intelligence.
